newsitem.title: USA: G. Gordon Liddy shunned from Ford Museum ceremony.
newsitem.headline: G. Gordon Liddy shunned from Ford Museum ceremony.

text.p: Former President Gerald Ford put some of his Watergate legacy on display Thursday but refused to welcome G. Gordon Liddy, the man who engineered the infamous political burglary.

Officials at the Gerald R. Ford Museum refused to allow Liddy to broadcast his nationally syndicated talk radio show from the museum grounds during the dedication of new exhibits here, which include pliers, screwdrivers, rubber gloves and other tools used in the 1972 Watergate Hotel break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters.
The incident ultimately led to the 1974 resignation of President Richard Nixon, thrusting Ford into the presidency.
The museum exhibit features a large black-and-white photo of Liddy chomping on a cigar, but Ford said he did not want the conservative talk show host crashing Thursday's party.
"He's a commercial news guy that wants to intrude," Ford said. "He can come into the public museum, but he's not a part of the ceremony."

But Liddy came to Grand Rapids anyway and broadcast his show from a local movie theatre. The former FBI agent, who spent 52 months in prison for his part in the burglary, said if it had not been for his actions, Ford would not have become president.
"I'm happy to say that I've got more tools in my home that they've got in their museum," Liddy quipped during the show.

Also conspicuously absent from the ceremonies was former President Ronald Reagan, who has been kept from public appearances by Alzheimer's disease. But Ford was joined by former Presidents Jimmy Carter and George Bush in the dedication, along with former First Ladies Betty Ford, Rosalynn Carter, Barbara Bush and Lady Bird Johnson.
The new exhibits at the museum are designed to provide a more interactive view of Ford's brief, 30-month presidency, which ended after Carter defeated him in the 1976 election.
"I think they've done a marvellous job of sort of embellishing my record," Ford said, quickly adding that it also includes many reminders of low points, such as the Watergate tools.
"Those tools us of a very tragic incident in American history," he said.
